title: Algebraic description of complex conjugation on cohomology of a smooth projective hypersurface

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The stated conclusion is \(\varphi_\mathbb C([y^i f_{j_i}])=\varphi_\mathbb C([y^{n-1-i}\widetilde f_{j_i}])\). But the two classes lie in different Hodge summands: the first is in \(H_0^{n-1-i,i}\), whereas the second is in \(H_0^{i,n-1-i}\). For \(i\ne (n-1)/2\), these are distinct direct summands, so nonzero classes cannot be equal. The stated goal immediately before the theorem is to find the complex conjugate of the first class, not an equal class. The theorem has omitted complex conjugation on one side (or otherwise states a false equality).

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 2.3, especially the passage from the single scalar \(U_{k,\gamma}\) to the assertion that \(\widetilde f_{j_i}\) is the conjugate representative
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof only establishes one scalar identity, \(\mathcal R(y^i f_{j_i},y^{n-1-i}\widetilde f_{j_i})=U_{k,\gamma}\), namely the pairing of the alleged conjugate with the original vector. This does not determine a vector in the complementary Hodge space when that space has dimension greater than one. To identify \(\overline{\phi(U_k)}\), one must match its pairings with a full basis (equivalently solve a Gram/period-matrix system), not merely its self-pairing with \(\phi(U_k)\). The formula (2.10) instead makes the answer a scalar multiple of an arbitrarily chosen \(g_{j_i}\). For example, hypersurfaces can have \(h^{n-1-i,i}>1\), so this cannot generally recover conjugation.

If conjugation exchanges \(U=y^i f\) and \(V=y^{n-1-i}\widetilde f\), then \(w=(U+V)/2\) is fixed by conjugation, but \(\sqrt{-1}w\) is sent to \(-\sqrt{-1}w\), not fixed. Hence \(\mathbb R[w]+\sqrt{-1}\mathbb R[w]\) is not a real Betti/de Rham structure (the fixed real subspace). The second real generator should involve the anti-invariant combination, e.g. \(\sqrt{-1}(U-V)/2\), rather than \(\sqrt{-1}(U+V)/2\). The same error is repeated in Example 2.8.

The theorem describes complex conjugation as satisfying \(H_0^{p,q}=H_0^{q,p}\). Hodge symmetry gives an antilinear isomorphism \(\overline{H_0^{p,q}}=H_0^{q,p}\), not equality of these subspaces inside \(H_0\). Except in the middle type \(p=q\), the summands are generally distinct. This false identification is also incompatible with the theorem's intended switch from weight \(i\) to weight \(n-1-i\).

The displayed expression \(\mu=(\int_{\gamma_1}\omega\cdot\int_{\gamma_2}\omega-\int_{\gamma_2}\omega\cdot\int_{\gamma_1}\omega)/(24\pi\sqrt{-1})\) is identically zero because the two period integrals are complex scalars and commute. It therefore cannot represent a nontrivial period/polarization coefficient. The formula also lacks the complex conjugation and/or intersection pairing appearing in Definition 2.2.

predicted_errors.error_location: Example 2.4, claim that \(\{[1],[yu]\}\) is a basis of \(\mathbb Q[y,x_0,x_1,x_2]/\operatorname{Jac}(S)\) for any cubic \(u\notin\operatorname{Jac}(S)\)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The full quotient \(A/\operatorname{Jac}(S)\) is not two-dimensional; the two displayed elements can at most be a basis of the charge-zero component relevant to the Griffiths description. Moreover, the stated condition on \(u\) is insufficient: for example \(u=x_0G_0\) need not lie in \(\operatorname{Jac}(S)=(G,yG_0,yG_1,yG_2)\) as a polynomial without \(y\), while \(yu=x_0(yG_0)\) does lie in \(\operatorname{Jac}(S)\). Thus \([yu]\) can vanish under the example's stated hypothesis. The needed condition is on the Jacobian-ring class of \(u\), not merely \(u\notin\operatorname{Jac}(S)\).

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.4 (odd \(n\)), definition of \(U_{k,\gamma}\) using \(P_X\,P\,\overline{P_X}^{T}\) and the claimed reuse of Theorem 2.3
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: For a non-unimodular homology intersection matrix \(P\), period vectors are coordinates obtained by evaluating cohomology on homology cycles. The induced cohomological cup-product pairing is obtained using the inverse intersection form (up to the fixed sign convention), not by multiplying the two period vectors by \(P\) itself. This matters here because the text explicitly states \(\det P=\pm e\), so generally \(P\) is not its own inverse. Consequently the asserted commutative pairing argument from the even-dimensional symplectic case cannot simply be reused with \(P_XP\overline{P_X}^T\), and the resulting odd-\(n\) conjugation formula is unsupported.

The text repeatedly relies on numbered references—for example, Griffiths [4], Carlson and Griffiths [1], and detailed claims attributed to [6, (12.5), (12.6), Remark (12.10)]—but provides no bibliography or bibliographic metadata at all. These attributions therefore cannot be checked, and the paper does not identify the sources needed to verify the cited formulas and conventions.
